title: Promises that build: the covenants

line.younger: God makes promises and keeps them. Seven pictures follow the covenants, from Noah's rainbow to the cup Jesus shared, each one laid on the one before like the stones of an arch.
line.older: The covenants through the whole Bible in seven pictures: Noah, Abraham, Sinai, David, the new covenant promised, the cup at the supper, and every promise kept in Christ.

poster: Green hills under a rainbow, and on the right an arch begun: its first stone in place, the rest of it drawn as a faint dotted outline.

frames.name: The bow in the clouds
frames.still: Green hills after rain under a rainbow drawn in three bands; on the right the first stone of an arch is set on the ground, a small bow cut into it.
frames.younger: After the flood, God made a promise to Noah, to his family and to every living creature: never again would a flood destroy the earth. God set his rainbow in the clouds as the sign. A promise like this, which God binds himself to keep, the Bible calls a covenant.
frames.older: A covenant is a binding relationship sealed by a solemn promise, often with a sign. The word first appears with Noah. After the flood God made his covenant with Noah, his descendants and “every living creature,” promising never again to destroy the earth by a flood, and set the rainbow as its sign. It rests on God's word alone: he will keep the world in which he will work out his rescue.

verse.text: I have set My rainbow in the clouds, and it will be a sign of the covenant between Me and the earth.

frames.name: Count the stars
frames.still: A tent under a night sky full of stars, and a man standing outside it looking up; on the right a second stone is set opposite the first, a star cut into it.
frames.younger: Later God made a covenant with Abram. He took him outside at night and told him to count the stars: his family would be as many as that, and through it every family on earth would be blessed. Abram believed God.
frames.older: With Abraham comes the promise everything after grows from: land, a family as many as the stars, and blessing for “all the families of the earth.” Abram believed, and it was “credited to him as righteousness.” Then God sealed the promise in an old form: in the dark a flaming torch passed between the halves of the offering, and God alone passed through, binding himself while Abram slept.

verse.text: And the LORD took him outside and said, “Now look to the heavens and count the stars, if you are able.” Then He told him, “So shall your offspring be.”

frames.name: Rescued, then the law
frames.still: A mountain wrapped in cloud, and in front of it two stone tablets standing side by side; a third stone is laid on the left side of the arch, two small tablets cut into it.
frames.younger: God rescued Abraham's family from slavery in Egypt. Then at Mount Sinai he made a covenant with the whole people and gave them his law. The rescue came first, and the law came after: they were to live as God's own treasured people.
frames.older: At Sinai God first reminds Israel of the rescue, “I carried you on eagles’ wings and brought you to Myself,” and only then offers the covenant: they will be his treasured possession, “a kingdom of priests and a holy nation.” Even the Ten Commandments begin with grace, not a demand: “I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt.”

verse.text: Now if you will indeed obey My voice and keep My covenant, you will be My treasured possession out of all the nations

frames.name: A throne for ever
frames.still: A throne on a hill with a line of small marks running from it across the picture and off its edge; a fourth stone is laid on the right side of the arch, a small crown cut into it.
frames.younger: Then God made a covenant with King David. He promised that a king from David's family would sit on his throne for ever.
frames.older: David wanted to build God a house. Instead God promised to build David a house: not a building but a family line, with a throne established for ever. Second Samuel 7 does not use the word covenant, but the psalms do: “I have made a covenant with My chosen one.” Every later hope for a king from David's line grows from this promise.

verse.text: Your house and kingdom will endure forever before Me, and your throne will be established forever.

frames.name: A new covenant promised
frames.still: Two stone tablets lie broken on the ground, and beside them a person stands with a small heart drawn on their chest, lines written inside it; a fifth stone is laid on the left of the arch, a heart cut into it.
frames.younger: But the people broke the covenant again and again, and at last they were taken far from home. Even then God made a new promise through the prophet Jeremiah: one day he would write his law on his people's hearts, and forgive them.
frames.older: Israel broke the covenant, the prophets brought God's case against them, and the exile came as the covenant had warned. Yet in the dark Jeremiah announced “a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah,” not like the one broken at Sinai: the law written on hearts, every person knowing God, and sins remembered no more.

verse.text: I will put My law in their minds and inscribe it on their hearts. And I will be their God, and they will be My people.

frames.name: The cup at the supper
frames.still: A table in an upper room with a loaf and a cup on it, a lamp in the window; at the top of the arch the sixth stone and the gold keystone, a cup, are set in place.
frames.younger: On the night before he died, Jesus ate the Passover meal with his friends. He took the cup and said that it was the new covenant, the one God had promised. Christians still remember his words whenever they share the bread and the cup.
frames.older: On the night before he died, at the Passover meal, Jesus took the cup and called it the new covenant. His words echo Moses at Sinai, “the blood of the covenant,” and Jeremiah's promise that sins will be forgiven: Jesus took his own death to be the sacrifice that sets up the covenant the prophets promised. The church has repeated his words at the Lord's Table ever since.

verse.text: This cup is the new covenant in My blood, which is poured out for you.

frames.name: Every promise kept
frames.still: The finished arch stands open like a gateway with light streaming through it, and people walk toward it along a path from the left.
frames.younger: God kept his promises in Jesus, and people from every nation are welcomed into God's family through him. God has not given up on the people he first made promises to: Paul says God's gifts and his call are never taken back. The story ends where it was always going, with God living among his people.
frames.older: Paul writes that all the promises of God are “Yes” in Christ. Hebrews calls the first covenant ‘obsolete’, but, as the Study Bible's notes on Hebrews say, these words are not a verdict that God has rejected the Jewish people. Paul asks, “did God reject His people? Certainly not!” The story ends as the first promises hoped: God with his people, and they his people.

verse.text: For all the promises of God are “Yes” in Christ.

think.younger: God keeps his promises, even when it takes a very long time. Which promise in this moving picture would you most like to remember?
think.older: Every covenant begins with what God gives before anything is asked: the rainbow, the stars, the rescue, the throne, the cup. Why might that order matter?

differ.text: Christians who hold different readings of the covenants agree that the whole Bible leads to Christ and that every promise of God is kept in him. They differ on how the covenants relate to each other and on how Israel and the church relate: covenant theology, dispensational readings, progressive covenantalism and new covenant theology each put it differently. None of them teaches that God has abandoned the Jewish people. This moving picture does not choose between them. The readings are set out in
